title: Experimental many-electron quantum states of real crystals

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a way to infer the electronic quantum state of a real crystal from experiments, with quantified uncertainty and enough information to distinguish competing descriptions of its electrons. Its ambition extends beyond locating atoms or fitting a spatial electron-density distribution: it seeks to constrain how electrons occupy states and correlate with one another in periodic solids, catalytic sites and crystalline macromolecules. Diffraction would provide central experimental constraints, supplemented by measurements sensitive to electronic distinctions that diffraction alone cannot resolve.

A crucial distinction is the difference between electron density, a one-particle density matrix and a full correlated many-electron state. Electron density describes the spatial distribution of charge. A one-particle density matrix contains additional information relevant to one-particle observables, but does not generally determine all correlations among electrons. Reconstructing it would therefore be a substantial intermediate achievement, while the title's full many-electron ambition would require additional correlation information or an explicit characterization of the states still compatible with the observations. This distinction incorporates the supplied review's scientific reasoning.

The research positions quantum crystallography as the starting point: it describes existing methods that refine aspherical electron densities and restrain calculated wavefunctions using diffraction. The proposed advance would make crystal-specific electronic-state inference experimentally discriminating and independently testable. The cited background review was not captured in the supplied source record, so these descriptions of existing capabilities are retained as research-reported context rather than independently verified findings.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability could turn some disagreements about electronic structure into experimentally decidable questions. Its direct power would be to distinguish descriptions that predict measurably different observables within stated uncertainties. For example, competing charge or spin descriptions could be discriminated only if the chosen measurements were sensitive to those differences. Agreement with a charge-density measurement alone would not establish that all competing spin or correlation descriptions had been excluded. This is a conditional impact assessment based on the supplied review.

The revolutionary consequence would be a stronger experimental basis for understanding bonding, charge redistribution and correlation in the actual crystalline environment. Validated one-particle inference could constrain one-particle properties; access to relevant higher-order correlations could support broader conclusions about correlated electronic behavior. The resulting evidence could improve electronic-structure models and help evaluate explanations of catalytic or material behavior, provided those explanations depend on distinctions the experiments actually resolve.

Further benefits for catalyst design, reaction prediction or devices would remain conditional. An experimentally constrained electronic state would not by itself determine a reaction rate or device performance: those outcomes can also depend on dynamics, temperature, defects, environment and other modeling assumptions. Likewise, orbital assignments require a stated representation and justification; they should not be presented as uniquely observed merely because a density model fits diffraction. The appropriate analogy is an expansion of experimentally constrained electronic knowledge, with scope defined by the measured systems and observables.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is an experimentally constrained, crystal-specific description that resolves the electronic distinctions of interest while exposing its remaining ambiguity. The research identifies an inverse problem: multiple physically admissible density matrices can share an electron density, so fitting that density cannot by itself certify a unique wavefunction. The supplied review adds that even identifying a one-particle density matrix would leave a further gap to full correlated-state determination. The research attributes the density-matrix discussion to section 2.3 of the 2017 quantum-crystallography review, whose text was not retained for verification.

Crystal-environment modeling is another barrier. A diffraction-restrained molecular wavefunction must account adequately for the surroundings when the target is the electronic state of the crystal. The research attributes a limitation in handling crystalline-environment effects to the 2024 work by Genoni and Martín Pendás. Because the source text is absent, the extent of that limitation and the methods to which it applies cannot be checked here. The engineering goal remains to state and validate the treatment of periodicity and environment rather than assume that a good density fit resolves them.

The research also identifies radiation damage, disorder and the collection of sufficiently detailed diffraction data as practical obstacles. It suggests that data extending to approximately 0.5 Å or finer may be needed for the intended inference, but the supplied evidence does not establish that value as a universal requirement or sufficient condition. The reported exceptionally high-resolution protein example illustrates the favorable end of the proposed experimental setting; it does not establish comparable feasibility across ordinary macromolecular crystals.

As a synthesis of the research and review, the methodological challenge is to combine complementary measurements without concealing dependence on theoretical assumptions. An independent observable such as a Compton profile could constrain information absent from spatial density alone, but its usefulness must be demonstrated for the particular competing states. A successful method would need uncertainty propagation, stated assumptions about whether the inferred density matrix corresponds to a physically possible electron system, and an account of which higher-order correlations remain unconstrained. Neither additional measurements nor a sophisticated fit automatically removes all state ambiguity.

current_state.text: The supplied research describes established quantum-crystallographic work on aspherical densities and diffraction-restrained wavefunctions, particularly for favorable small molecules. It cites Grabowsky, Genoni and Bürgi's 2017 Chemical Science review, volume 8, page 4159, as background and as the source for density-matrix nonuniqueness. No saved text or source artifact accompanies that citation. These are therefore reported capabilities and theoretical context from the research, with their precise scope unverified in the supplied review.

For 2024, the research cites Genoni and Martín Pendás in the Journal of Chemical Physics, volume 160, article 234108, DOI 10.1063/5.0213247, with an acceptance date of 3 June 2024. It attributes to that paper a continuing difficulty in accounting effectively for the crystalline environment in X-ray-restrained wavefunction methods. The review could not check this characterization against source text. Even if verified, a limitation reported in that work would describe its relevant scope and date; it would not alone establish the state of every subsequent method.

The research reports that Paknia, Chari and co-authors published a Pyrococcus abyssi rubredoxin structure at 0.43 Å resolution, online on 12 August 2026, in Acta Crystallographica D, DOI 10.1107/S2059798326007448. It says bonding density was accounted for using a transferable aspherical-atom model and reports that, as of 9 May 2026, only 20 PDB entries lay between 0.5 and 0.7 Å. These numerical and methodological details are preserved as reported, but the article text and the basis of the database count were not captured, so they remain unverified. If confirmed, the result would demonstrate exceptional protein diffraction and density modeling; it would not by itself demonstrate correlated many-electron-state reconstruction.

The research also points to the IUCr's 2025 quantum-crystallography collection, identifying an IUCrJ contribution in volume 12, pages 610–613, DOI 10.1107/S2052252525008759. It interprets the collection as evidence of an active research field. The supplied URL is an issue page, and no retained text establishes the contents or completeness of the relevant contribution. A thematic collection alone would not demonstrate a general quantum-state measurement capability.

Across all four citations, the supplied source index contains no captured documents or extraction artifacts. That limits verification; it is not evidence that the reported results are false. Separately, no bounded freshness search was supplied to establish developments through 1 November 2026. The record therefore supports presenting the innovation as a proposed capability with reported partial precedents, while leaving its latest general status unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed first demonstration: select a periodic solid with competing electronic descriptions and publish a diffraction-constrained one-particle density matrix with quantified uncertainty and explicit physical-representability assumptions. Require agreement, within stated errors, with the measured density, an independently measured observable such as a Compton profile, and a pre-registered electronic property. The demonstration should identify which competing descriptions the observations distinguish and which remain compatible. These are proposed criteria, not established field standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed first demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed second demonstration: apply the same inference and validation principles separately to an enzyme active site, stating how the surrounding macromolecule and crystal affect the result. An exceptionally well-diffracting small protein would be a useful intermediate milestone. Fitting bonding density through transferable multipoles or an aspherical-atom library would not alone meet the proposed state-inference criterion, because successful density modeling need not identify the electronic state.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed second demonstration

completion_criteria.text: A claim to the full many-electron ambition would additionally need experimental constraints on the relevant higher-order correlations, or an explicit account of the remaining many-electron ambiguity and its consequences. Agreement of a one-particle density matrix with density, a Compton profile and one property would establish validated predictions within that test; it would not generally establish complete correlated-state reconstruction. If only a restricted set of states can be distinguished, the claimed achievement should state that restriction.
completion_criteria.label: A claim to the full many-electron ambition would

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements include releasing the measured data, inference procedure, assumptions and uncertainty analysis in enough detail for independent reconstruction, followed by replication on independent measurements or specimens. Practical boundaries should include resolution, radiation exposure, disorder, sample requirements and sensitivity to environment modeling. Tests across additional crystals and electronic regimes could establish increasing demonstrated breadth. A finite collection of successful tests would not establish literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility requirements include releasing the measured data,

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CRX-01, “Atomic-resolution imaging of a single non-crystalline molecule before destruction,” and CRX-08, “Ab initio atomic structure of matter that exists only once,” share the challenge of extracting information before a specimen is lost. Their stated targets are atomic structure in single-object or nonrepeatable settings. CRX-05 instead targets electronic-state information in real crystals; recovering atomic positions, even exceptionally well, would not by itself determine electron correlations.

Roster-based synthesis: CRX-02, “Chemically complete atomic structures of bulk amorphous solids,” and CRX-04, “Atomic ensembles measured from total X-ray scattering,” overlap through difficult inverse problems and the need to describe structural ambiguity. CRX-02 concerns noncrystalline atomic structure, while CRX-04 concerns atomic ensembles. CRX-05 concerns electronic states in crystals. Structural ensembles and electronic-state uncertainty may interact, but they are distinct reconstruction targets.

Roster-based synthesis: CRX-03, “Chemical-accuracy prediction of which molecular crystal will form,” and CRX-07, “Predictive experimental selection of a chosen crystal form,” concern crystal formation and selection. Better experimental electronic constraints could help assess models relevant to those problems, but would not alone solve relative free energies, nucleation or growth. Conversely, predicting or selecting a crystal form would not establish its correlated electronic state.

Roster-based synthesis: CRX-06, “Atomic movies of elementary chemical steps without a photo-trigger,” adds time-resolved structural information. CRX-05 could complement such movies by constraining electronic descriptions, but a validated state at one condition would not establish a reaction pathway or rate. CRX-09, “Protonation state as a routine crystallographic observable,” overlaps more directly with charge distribution and active-site interpretation. Protonation is a narrower chemical assignment and need not require full many-electron reconstruction.

Roster-based synthesis: CRX-10, “Laboratory sources that do facility-class coherent X-ray crystallography,” CRX-11, “Diffraction-quality crystals of arbitrary macromolecules on demand,” and CRX-13, “A growth rulebook that suppresses defects, twins, and disorder in arbitrary crystals,” address source access and specimen quality. Progress could expand the samples and data available for CRX-05. These enabling improvements would still leave the electronic inverse problem, correlation ambiguity and independent validation to be solved.

Roster-based synthesis: CRX-12, “Continuous atomic-resolution crystallography inside working devices and static extreme environments,” overlaps with CRX-05's need to describe the actual environment of a crystal. Combining them could enable electronic-state inference under operating conditions, if suitable observables and sample quality were available. CRX-12's stated atomic-resolution structural capability and CRX-05's electronic-state capability remain separate achievements.

change_log.change: Preserved CRX-05 and its original title while distinguishing electron density, one-particle density matrices and full correlated many-electron states.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent, but the proposed one-particle output does not generally determine the full state named in the title.

change_log.change: Narrowed the direct significance to discrimination among electronic descriptions distinguishable by measured observables and their uncertainties.
change_log.reason: The earlier claim that measurement would decide electronic-structure arguments was broader than the proposed evidence could establish.

change_log.change: Integrated charge and spin sensitivity, orbital interpretation, higher-order correlations and downstream modeling limits into the relevant sections.
change_log.reason: These useful review distinctions explain what electronic inference could establish and what would require additional justification.

change_log.change: Retained the experimental barriers and approximate 0.5 Å scale while qualifying the numerical scale as unverified and nonuniversal.
change_log.reason: The research identifies useful feasibility concerns, but the supplied evidence does not establish a general resolution threshold.

change_log.change: Preserved the reported 2024 limitation, 2026 rubredoxin result, 0.43 Å resolution, dated PDB count and 2025 collection with explicit source-access qualifications.
change_log.reason: Missing source artifacts prevent verification without demonstrating that those reports are false.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstrations to include uncertainty, representability assumptions, discrimination between alternatives and remaining correlation ambiguity.
change_log.reason: This aligns the completion claims with what one-particle inference and finite validation could actually demonstrate.

change_log.change: Added proposed reproducibility requirements and practical applicability boundaries.
change_log.reason: Convincing completion requires independent reconstruction and replication, with claims bounded by tested systems and conditions.

unresolved_issues: All four source-index entries lack captured text or artifacts; their identities, relevant passages and retained-copy completeness cannot be verified from this record.
The precise scope of existing diffraction-restrained wavefunction capabilities and the 2024 crystalline-environment limitation remains unverified.
The reported 0.43 Å rubredoxin result, transferable-model interpretation, publication metadata and count of 20 PDB entries between 0.5 and 0.7 Å as of 9 May 2026 require source verification.
The approximate 0.5 Å experimental scale has not been established here as necessary or sufficient for any defined class of electronic-state inference.
The measurements and higher-order correlation constraints sufficient to distinguish the intended many-electron states remain unspecified.
The feasibility of the proposed independent-observable tests, particularly for enzyme active sites, has not been demonstrated by the supplied evidence.
No supplied freshness search establishes whether subsequent work achieved a broader capability by 1 November 2026.
The historical item invoked in the research was not supplied, so its comparison cannot be assessed.
